sources_considered.why: A Stocktwits report on Yahoo Finance relaying the Financial Times's independent check of the audited 2024 and 2025 net losses. It also gives the FT's figure excluding non-cash items.
Independent news summary that notes the FT verification and the FT's adjusted loss of about $8 billion. Used as context.

evidence_items.publisher: Stocktwits via Yahoo Finance (relaying the Financial Times)

receipt.public_excerpt: OpenAI's net loss ballooned from $5 billion in 2024 to a staggering $39 billion last year

evidence_items.explanation: The FT, working separately from the speaker, reports that audited net loss rose from about $5 billion in 2024 to about $39 billion in 2025. That is about a 7.8-fold rise, which meets the plain reading of a dramatic year-over-year increase.

evidence_items.publisher: Stocktwits via Yahoo Finance (relaying the Financial Times)
evidence_items.locator: section 'OpenAI's Loss Widened Due To Restructuring', paragraph 2

receipt.public_excerpt: The majority of the increase in net loss last year was due to non-cash accounting charges tied to the company's prior structure rather than its underlying operations

evidence_items.explanation: Most of the headline rise came from a one-time non-cash charge. Elsewhere the same report gives an adjusted 2025 loss of about $8 billion. On an underlying basis, the growth is much smaller than the headline multiple. This limits how much the 'dramatic' rate reflects operations.

receipt.public_excerpt: OpenAI’s losses for 2025 were closer to $8 billion once you strip out all of the stuff that should be one-time costs.

evidence_items.explanation: A second outlet confirms the FT's adjusted loss of about $8 billion. That figure is not on the same basis as the headline net loss the speaker cites.

unresolved_gaps: OpenAI has not published its financial statements. Its stock-market listing filing was confidential as of the evaluation date. The figures come from leaked audited documents that the FT verified.
No 2024 loss figure on an adjusted (non-cash-excluded) basis was found, so underlying growth cannot be measured exactly.
Only two years of audited figures were reported, so a longer year-over-year trend cannot be checked.
